Is it an experience centered on trading or stockpiling resources, or one that explores the extreme moral dilemmas of life and death, selfishness and selflessness, or perhaps one that builds an emotional connection between you and a particular character in a post-apocalyptic world?Even within the same post-apocalyptic setting, these experiences don’t have to be mutually exclusive. For instance, you could dedicate 30 percent of the experience to resource management and 70 percent to extreme moral dilemmas. These aspects must be understood through structural design from the very beginning; only then does the script come into play.
Q: From what I’ve heard, does AltFlow mainly help you set up the framework?
Kunpeng: Yes, that’s its most important value.It will assist you in writing the script, but scriptwriting isn’t the most important part. For example, when breaking down an IP: What are the character relationships and core experiences inherent to this subject matter? What kinds of interactions can occur between characters? Are they strategic or relational? What is the nature of these interactions—trust-based or resource-based? All of these aspects can be adjusted.
You can also adjust the pace of the interactions—making them more frequent at the beginning and less frequent toward the end—as well as set the proportions and values for different interaction types. Then, generate an outline, move on to the interaction script, and finally to video generation. If you feel something isn’t quite right along the way—for example, if a particular section isn’t exciting enough—you can change the direction, and it will rewrite the script accordingly.
Q: You mentioned "pleasure points." Can AI understand this concept, which serves human emotions and consciousness?
Kunpeng: AI is understandable because you feed it a large volume of scripts, and our professional team annotates them. This brings us to the issue of AI data: what kind of data anchors should you provide? Take blind testing, for example—humans need to give it feedback, otherwise it won’t know what “good” means.We generate two versions of the same content and have testers rate them: which one is better, whether it’s usable, and what the quality is like—but the testers don’t know which model wrote it.After repeated training and feedback, it becomes increasingly clear on these judgments. It knows what each model is capable of, and even which one excels at each step—which is better at branch design, and which is faster at advancing the plot.
Q: Are there already creators using this platform? Have you seen any particularly impressive ways it’s being used?
Kunpeng: During the testing phase, we released several hundred beta invitation codes to let creators try it out first; we haven’t started commercializing it to the public yet.I’ve seen some pretty interesting ways people are using it. For example, someone wrote their life story as a short biography and put it into the editor to generate branching choices—it’s kind of like using it to “tell fortunes.” I think that’s pretty funny.
Q: So it's not just a platform for making video games.
Kunpeng: Right. My ultimate conclusion is that it should be a “world.” Everyone is talking about open worlds, “Westworld,” and world models these days… but my view is that “Westworld” isn’t just about mountains, rivers, and the like—it has another very important aspect: the characters, relationships, events, and stories within it are constantly in motion.When interactive storytelling reaches its pinnacle, life itself becomes interactive storytelling—what I’m saying to you right now, whether I choose to say A or B next—choices are constantly present in life.Choice is the smallest unit through which humans engage with the world, and making a choice is essentially a form of annotation: what you like, what you don’t like, and what your preferences are at this very moment. When the choices generated by an infinite number of people, characters, and stories are all converted into data annotations, they can potentially become the model and agent that best understands “how a story should be written.” After all, stories are a timeless form of human emotional expression.
Broadly speaking, interactive movies and games are just one application of interactive storytelling, as are interactive short dramas.In the future, it could integrate more deeply with the gaming industry, with world models, and even with the kind of futuristic technology seen in *Ready Player One*—or with brain-computer interfaces. Ultimately, you still need a way to let users participate, make choices, and determine the course of the story. And the story paths users want to see are, in and of themselves, the highest-quality data.
03
The tipping point has been reached
Q: I’m curious about something. These days, people tend to instinctively view traditional short dramas and animated series as distinct from so-called “AI short dramas” and “AI animated series.” Will a similar situation arise with interactive video?
Kunpeng: I don’t think the distinction is that clear-cut. It’s just like the gaming industry: art is essentially just a medium used to convey what the creator truly wants to express.I think of AI as a virtual film set—it’s a virtual space for filming and production; on-location, real-world filming takes place on a tangible, physical set. Everyone does their own filming and expresses their own content.
It’s just that AI-generated content isn’t quite good enough yet—it still feels very “AI-like,” which is why we refer to it specifically as “AI content.” But as time goes on, I feel that this distinction has become very blurred. We’ve been conducting internal tests, and some of the recent results are so convincing that it’s hard to tell them apart from those created by real people.
Q: What exactly is being tested in this internal test?
Kunpeng: What we're measuring is when that so-called tipping point will arrive—the point at which we can use AI to generate content.
Q: As mentioned earlier, when you began focusing heavily on AI in 2023, were your employees eager to embrace it from the very beginning?
Kunpeng: It’s actually a process that’s both top-down and bottom-up—the two approaches converged. But at first, people were resistant because AI wasn’t good enough back then—which is perfectly understandable; it really wasn’t good enough at the beginning. It wasn’t until we kept trying that we realized it had actually become good enough.After June of last year, things changed dramatically: People began to realize that this technology had moved beyond the realm of concepts, demos, cost reduction, or preliminary materials and conceptual designs—it had truly become an “AI employee” capable of helping you get work done. By that point, people started using it on their own initiative.
Q: That makes sense—after all, people who create content tend to have high standards for it.
Kunpeng: Yes. So, taking our AltFlow as an example, I don’t see it as a replacement for creators. AI is there to empower creators, allowing them to focus on delivering a great user experience. As for some of the foundational tasks—such as writing flowcharts or designing branching paths—AI can handle them for you or provide excellent suggestions.I think with our current AI capabilities, AI can solve 70% to 80% of the problems, while the remaining 20% to 30% comes down to the creator’s inspiration—and that’s what’s most important about the creator themselves.
Q: In what directions will interactive content evolve in the coming years?
Kunpeng: I think there are three fairly clear directions.
First, greater social interaction. The evolution of games has followed a path from single-player to multiplayer, from offline to online, and finally to MMORPGs—becoming increasingly social. The same will be true for interactive content. By developing a two-player product, we aim to explore how social interaction will transform interactive storytelling.
Second, deeper integration with AI. AI will help creators better balance rational design and intuitive creativity, reduce costs, and empower everyone to explore topics they previously couldn’t afford to tackle.
Third, the formats will become more diverse. Interactive content shouldn’t be limited to live-action interactive games on Steam that last four or five hundred minutes. Shorter content, real-time live-streamed interactions, and procedurally generated content could all become new formats.
Q: What do you think the future of interactive storytelling will look like?
Kunpeng: I think a lot of science fiction works have actually already shown us this ultimate outcome—“Inception” is about creating dreams, allowing you to enter a world; “The Matrix” is about truly entering another reality through an interface; and in “Westworld,” every character has their own story, the entire world keeps running, and you’re the protagonist in it all.
I think interactive content in the future will be more like your very own “Westworld.” The IPs you love and the events that interest you can all be brought to life through AI and interaction, and you’ll be the protagonist in that world. You’ll no longer just passively consume stories—you’ll be able to truly participate in them.
I think that day is already very close. At the very least, if we set aside the more complex gameplay aspects and focus solely on the story, characters, and content generation, it’s already much closer than it used to be.
html:
Kunpeng is the kind of founder who has his vision ingrained in his very bones.

Ten years ago, he played games like *Heavy Rain*, *Beyond: Two Souls*, and Telltale’s *The Walking Dead*, and was captivated by interactive storytelling for the first time. He subsequently founded HuYing Technology—“HuYing”—which they later defined as “interactive film and television.”During a recent chat with me, he recommended *Unhinged*, an interactive horror series Netflix released a while back. In one scene, the protagonist can actually call the viewer directly on their cell phone. When he talks about moments like these, his speech still unconsciously speeds up, revealing the same excitement he felt back then.

Kun Peng, CEO of HuYing Technology, at the ChinaJoy 2026 Official Forum

Recently, news that *Prosperous World* had sold 5 million copies brought the interactive film and gaming genre back into the public eye, with major companies like ByteDance and Tencent collectively investing in this sector. The Dataeye Research Institute predicts that this genre is currently experiencing explosive growth, with an expected increase of over 90% compared to two years ago.

Data Source: Dataeye Research Institute

Kunpeng was very pleased: “People are finally recognizing the charm and value of interactive storytelling, which will attract more talented creators and entrepreneurs to the field—that’s exactly what I want to see.”

Over the past decade, they have defined several key turning points in the domestic interactive media industry.

HuYing’s 2019 release, *Antiques Bureau: The Origin of the Buddha’s Head*, is considered the pioneering work of interactive drama in China;In 2022, they partnered with Bilibili, bringing together well-known content creators such as Xiaoyao Sanren and C-Jiao, along with over 3 million users, to participate in *Super Raccoon Vote*, allowing viewers to influence the outcome of a battle royale through millions of bullet comments;Most well-known in the gaming community is the interactive film-game *Escape from Room 13*, which sold over a million copies; HuYing’s products have accumulated more than 10 million paying users worldwide.

"Flying Over Room 13"

A while back, they also launched pre-orders on the App Store for a brand-new interactive movie called *New World: Shadows in Tandem*, which focuses on two-player collaboration. With two players and two screens, you work together to decide the story’s direction.

From VR/AR and danmaku interactions to interactive movies and games, and from single-player to multiplayer modes, they’ve experimented with every form of interaction. Having navigated so many pitfalls, they’ve come to truly appreciate the blood, sweat, and tears that go into creating interactive experiences.So these days, while Kunpeng is pleased to see the category he’s been cultivating for years finally gaining traction, he also feels a strong sense of anxiety.

Creation, production, and distribution—these three major hurdles stand in the way of interactive film and game development: On the one hand, a good interactive film or game must have a compelling story and script;at the same time, it must contend with filming costs that can easily reach tens of thousands per minute; pre-production is highly intertwined with post-production gameplay mechanics, allowing for only a single take, which makes subsequent revisions extremely difficult; and the final product cannot succeed without effective distribution channels. Mutual Media has personally scaled all three of these mountains.

In Kunpeng’s view, these are long-standing, fundamental issues across the entire category—ones that won’t be automatically resolved just because the industry has become a hot trend—until the emergence of AI provided an opportunity to break the deadlock.

Kunpeng once used the metaphor of “a call from God.” AI is exactly that kind of call—it has the potential to multiply the growth of an entire product category by 10 or 100 times. It’s not just about reducing costs and shortening timelines; more importantly, it makes entirely new forms of experience possible.

Over the past year, Kunpeng has been busy driving this AI transformation within the company: many day-to-day operational and creative tasks have been taken over by “AI employees.”They are also testing AltFlow, an AI-powered interactive narrative creation platform—one designed to do just one thing: assist creators in developing interactive narratives and scripts. It doesn’t write the story for you; instead, it helps you build the framework: the kind of experience you want to create for users determines how you should write the story.

They found that, through blind testing and data annotation, AI has already learned to understand highly subjective human concepts such as “pleasure points” and “emotions.” Kun Peng said that AI can solve 70% to 80% of the problems, while the rest depends on the creator’s inspiration—which is what matters most to the creator.

Kunpeng showed me an AI interactive project they’re about to unveil to the public. It has some elements that show promise for breaking into the mainstream and capturing people’s attention. I tried to spot the “AI vibe” in the clips, but wasn’t very successful—and that might actually be the most noteworthy aspect.Prior to this, Huying had been conducting various “threshold” tests internally—not to measure model performance scores, but to pinpoint that critical point: the moment when AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from content shot by a real person.

And now, Kunpeng felt that the time had come.

The following is a transcript of a conversation between Tea House and Kun Peng, CEO of Huying Technology (some content has been edited for readability):

01

Regrets After a Million-Person Experiment

Teahouse Guy (hereinafter referred to as "Q"): Have you been developing interactive film and gaming experiences ever since you started your company?

Kunpeng: To be more precise, we’ve been constantly exploring and experimenting with various forms of interactive content. In the very beginning, we didn’t even call it “interactive film and gaming”—we called it “interactive drama.” Projects like *Antiques Bureau: The Origin of the Buddha’s Head*, as well as our attempts to make variety shows and film and television content interactive, were all developed during that phase.

"Antiques: The Origin of the Buddha's Head" was an interactive drama we created back then. It featured not only branching choices but also simulated actions, swipes, rapid taps, puzzle-solving, and how different choices affected subsequent character relationships and the plot’s direction. For example, if you treated a character a certain way earlier on, they might not come back to save you later in the story.There were also puzzle-solving mechanics based on the Nine Palaces and the Eight Trigrams, and the game featured multiple endings. Interestingly, this product was developed in 2018 and launched in January 2019. Many of the interactive features we wanted to implement back then still can’t be achieved on some platforms even today.

After that, since our interactive content was hosted on long-form video platforms and users hadn’t yet developed a habit of paying for such content, we began shifting our focus to the consumer market (To C) and released our product on gaming platforms like Steam.*Fly Over Room 13* was our first true consumer-facing product. It performed well in terms of sales, virality, and feedback from streamers—many streamers featured it—and it allowed us to confirm for the first time that users were willing to pay directly for this type of content.

Q: What’s it like to stick with something for ten years?

Kunpeng: I don’t think the word “perseverance” is entirely accurate here. To be honest, we didn’t really think about whether we needed to “persevere” or endure the process with great difficulty. Of course, there were many challenges along the way, but many of us on the team are gamers ourselves, and we also love interactive storytelling.We also place a strong emphasis on the immediacy and realism that live-action filming brings, which means the game team has to understand film production, and the film team has to understand interactivity and game design. We had to learn and figure out a lot of things on our own.

So if we absolutely have to use the word “perseverance,” I think the reason behind it is still passion.

Q: So, am I correct in understanding that the team’s core expertise lies in games and interaction design, and that it’s expanding into the film and television industry?

Kunpeng: Our team is quite multidisciplinary and highly diverse. It includes a film and television storytelling team, a game design team, and a technical development team.Within the technical team, we have a PhD in Human-Computer Interaction from Tsinghua University, an architect who graduated from Tsinghua’s Yao Class, a former architect from Hulu, and product managers with experience at major tech companies; we also have game designers and producers who have worked on titles that have sold over a million copies.

Bringing together people from all walks of life is actually a great opportunity to explore the next generation of storytelling—the next generation of personalized storytelling. I believe that’s exactly what we’re doing. Ever since we started working on *Antiques Bureau: The Origin of the Buddha’s Head*, we’ve been conducting various in-house technical explorations, such as 360-degree VR experiences, interactive video players, and video formats.

Q: Are there any interesting examples of exploration?

Kunpeng: Yes, and we’ve even won some gaming awards for it. We’ve found that interactive content isn’t limited to the narrative-driven products we just mentioned—there are also more entertaining, game-like directions to explore.In 2022, right around the time *Squid Game* was taking the world by storm, we collaborated with Bilibili on an interactive AI-based game called *Super Raccoon Vote*: Users posted comments in real time and cast votes to influence the plot’s direction as it unfolded.

At the time, there were many specific technical challenges to overcome: How do we enable real-time interaction with a million users online? How do we tally votes and compile statistics despite some latency? How do we allow 30 to 60 live streams and ten incoming links to participate in this content simultaneously?Not only did we need to build a backend real-time decision-making and voting system—back then, there wasn’t the kind of real-time content generation technology we have today—but our approach was to stack various plot trees using a massive library of assets, store them in the cloud, and let users’ decisions determine what content was broadcast. Think of it this way: there’s a massive cloud-based asset library that distributes different content based on users’ “battle royale”-style decisions.

Q: What did you learn from this test?

Kunpeng: The biggest takeaway was confirming that real-time multiplayer interaction is a viable direction, and player engagement was incredibly high. But at that point, the technology wasn’t ready yet.

Back then, there weren’t any generative tools like Sora or Seedance. But the creative freedom offered by live-action filming is ultimately limited—you can’t film every possible scenario, and it’s impossible to exhaust all possibilities. We shot a huge amount of footage and uploaded it to the cloud to provide users with real-time feedback, but I felt it wasn’t enough—it couldn’t achieve true personalization.

I believe that whether it’s interactive live streams, interactive videos, interactive dramas, or interactive movies and games, the essence of interactivity is to provide users with a personalized experience. However, within existing content formats, we can’t simulate exactly what every user wants in terms of a personalized experience, so we have to settle for a compromise: filming with real people and giving users some options.

This part really puts the creator's skills to the test. You have to represent the vast majority of people as much as possible and figure out what they want.You can’t possibly cater to everyone, so focus on what kind of experience the vast majority of people want from interactive storytelling, and build your product based on your experience and insights. But this is difficult—you can’t cover every angle, and there will always be some areas where the option design or interactive storytelling experience falls short. This has long been the most frustrating aspect of this industry for us.

That is precisely why we believe the fundamental issues with interactive storytelling have not been resolved.

Q: What does “the fundamental issues of interactive narrative” refer to?

Kunpeng: Let me break it down into three points.

The production phase is probably where the industry feels the impact the most. The volume of footage required for interactive video is enormous, and the cost per project is too high—it’s simply impossible to fully explore all the narrative possibilities within a limited budget. If the art style in a game isn’t right, you can scrap it and start over; but with interactive video, you can only shoot it once, and once it’s done, you can’t make changes—not even by spending more money, unless you’re willing to spend a great deal of it.

The second point is distribution. Previously, distribution was significantly constrained by platforms, but now it’s relatively more flexible. Soon, our video format will also be integrated into various domestic apps, mini-programs, and other platforms, allowing interactive content to play directly on these platforms. It’s quite important to ensure that domestic players can enjoy the interactive content as intended.

The third point—and the most challenging one—is the creative process: writing a good interactive script is extremely difficult. It requires a balance between rational and emotional thinking, which calls for collaboration between the game development team and the film and television production team. It’s not just about writing a script; it’s about crafting an entire interactive experience.

With layer upon layer of hurdles piling up, this industry is like a giant funnel that constantly sifts through candidates. In the end, only a very small number of teams remain—those that have truly dedicated themselves to the field for many years, have accumulated deep expertise, and continue to invest in research.

02

When AI Becomes a Game-Changer in Film and Gaming: This Time, It’s Really Different

Q: So do you think the interactive film and video genre has reached its ceiling? Not long ago, everyone was talking about the boom in the interactive film and game sector, with some titles selling millions of copies. What stage do you think interactive film and games are currently in?

Kunpeng: We’re nowhere near hitting a ceiling; I think the film-to-game adaptation trend in China is actually just getting started.People will gradually get used to seeing new things. The team behind *Prosperous Realm* is amazing—they’re truly passionate about this field. What they’ve discovered is that female-oriented content can sell very well, and it’s no longer limited to the gaming community; it’s broken into the TV drama and broader content consumption markets.Our *Flying Over Room 13* is a social-realism title aimed at Steam players and international audiences; and *New World: Shadows in Tandem* explores an interactive film-game experience similar to *It Takes Two*. Film-games are actually breaking through traditional genre boundaries, becoming increasingly mainstream and widespread.

"New World: Shadows in Pairs"

Interactivity also requires more content and more people from various industries to get involved, using more works to educate the market. The same goes for short-form dramas—people didn’t start loving them overnight; instead, their viewing habits developed gradually. At first, people said, “Aren’t short-form dramas just longer series cut into shorter segments?” but now the mindset is completely different.

Let me give you some figures: on just one platform alone, tens of thousands of short dramas are released each month in China; the annual box office revenue for the film market is 50 billion yuan.We have products that have sold over a million copies, but compared to the existing short-form drama, film, or gaming markets, interactive film and gaming remains very small. It still has enormous potential and is a sector on the rise.

Then there are the changes brought about by AI. I’d like to return to the question you raised earlier: I sense that core AI technologies are already tackling those three fundamental challenges in interactive content. That’s why we feel that this time, things really seem different—not just because new blockbusters, new products, and new business models are drawing attention to this sector, but because some fundamental challenges may actually be getting resolved.For example, AI can transform what used to be a nearly “one-time” filming and production process into an iterative model similar to game development. It can also significantly reduce production costs, making high-budget genres like fantasy and xianxia feasible.

Q: When did you start taking an interest in AI?

Kunpeng: We started using AI for some experimental projects back in 2023. At the time, I really wanted to test something: I’m a huge fan of the *Xianjian Qixia Zhuan* IP, so I wondered if we could use AI to recreate it—to have Li Xiaoyao rescue Zhao Ling’er.People already have such strong associations and impressions of these characters—who played them and what they looked like are etched in everyone’s minds—that it would be very difficult to recreate this with live-action actors; it would always feel a bit unsatisfying.So we used AI to create videos. But to be honest, it never made it to market—the AI technology at the time wasn’t advanced enough. There were obvious hallucination issues, and the video footage was shaky, so it wasn’t really market-ready; it was more of a demo test.

Starting in 2024, we gradually began doing a bit more. By the first half of 2025, we started using more video models like Veo, still with the goal of addressing the content shortage. By mid-2025, there were actually already many video models capable of producing high-quality videos. However, video production merely reduces costs; it doesn’t truly solve the industry’s problems.

What really moved me was the creative process. In June 2025, when “vibe coding”—writing code with AI—started to take off, we began to wonder: Could we use the “vibe” approach to create something—to use AI for creative work? I gave it a try myself and used AI to write an interactive story.Wow—I thought it seemed kind of interesting; it actually worked. At first, we used an internal system we’d written ourselves—not the AI tool we have now—and after testing it, we found it was pretty cool.

So in the second half of last year—around August or September—we started working on an agent. The large language model’s training data didn’t include interactive scripts, so it didn’t understand what “interaction” meant or what constituted good interactive design—it might not even be able to write a novel well, let alone create interactive content.So we began fine-tuning it, adding a multi-path routing system and the ability to parse IP, and gradually realized that this approach might actually work. We’ve been conducting continuous experiments since 2023, and by the second half of last year, we had truly integrated AI into our operations on a comprehensive basis.

Q: How are you currently using AI internally?

Kunpeng: We’re all moving toward AI—not just programmers, designers, artists, and backend developers… Every team is using it to boost efficiency. I think this is an inevitable trend; it’s not mandatory—if people find it useful, they’ll adopt it on their own.

For example, when we use AI to “break down” a novel’s plot, it’s a bit like having 64 AI units “read” the book for you.When a novel comes in, humans read it too slowly, so we have different large language models work together—Model A specializes in analyzing structure, Model B in plot, and Model C in dialogue. Each AI unit has its own specific role, and when combined, they form a virtual team that helps us get a lot of work done.

Our team has been continuously exploring this field, venturing into new and uncharted territory. We are currently developing AltFlow, an AI agent product for interactive storytelling. In fact, we want to make the AI capabilities we’ve developed internally available to everyone, because interactive storytelling is truly not something that can be done well by just one team.

I think the biggest problem in the interactive content industry right now is a lack of production capacity; we need more talented creators and excellent teams to join the field. In the past, the industry was too small and the market was too limited. Whether it was due to creative challenges, high production costs, or high barriers to distribution, many issues kept smart people from getting involved in this field.But with more high-quality products emerging this year—and following the success of some of our products last year—people are starting to take notice of this sector. If we can also take this opportunity to lower the barriers to entry, then this venture will become viable.

Q: As a company with extensive experience in film and game production, what makes your approach to developing an AI-powered film and game creation platform different?

Kunpeng: The hardest part of this industry is the creative process. We focus on one thing: using AI to assist in the creation of interactive narratives. Interactive storytelling is inherently challenging—it involves many steps—and most people don’t truly understand the real needs of creators. But because we’ve been serving these creators for a long time, we understand the problems they’re trying to solve.There are already plenty of tools for video generation; that’s not where the challenge lies.

Q: You mentioned earlier that creating interactive narratives is very challenging. In what specific ways is that the case?

Kunpeng: Our producer might explain this more professionally than I can—many people think interactive storytelling is just about writing a script and then creating multiple endings, but that’s not actually the case.The kind of experience you want to create for users determines how you write the story and design the interactions—it’s not about starting with a linear story. The creative process begins with the user experience, not just with the story itself.

Q: How does AltFlow speed up this creative process?

Kunpeng: It has two modes. One is guided, which provides you with workflows and helps you break down the process from a “Flow” perspective—this is a step-by-step method that shows you how to break down interactive content.The other is free mode, which lets you explore freely and expand any pre-written script or idea you have into an interactive experience.

One point it repeatedly emphasizes is: What is your experience? For example, in a post-apocalyptic setting, it doesn’t stop at very concrete choices like “save or not save.”There are many types of post-apocalyptic settings—what kind of experience do you want to create? Is it an experience centered on trading or stockpiling resources, or one that explores the extreme moral dilemmas of life and death, selfishness and selflessness, or perhaps one that builds an emotional connection between you and a particular character in a post-apocalyptic world?Even within the same post-apocalyptic setting, these experiences don’t have to be mutually exclusive. For instance, you could dedicate 30 percent of the experience to resource management and 70 percent to extreme moral dilemmas. These aspects must be understood through structural design from the very beginning; only then does the script come into play.

Q: From what I’ve heard, does AltFlow mainly help you set up the framework?

Kunpeng: Yes, that’s its most important value.It will assist you in writing the script, but scriptwriting isn’t the most important part. For example, when breaking down an IP: What are the character relationships and core experiences inherent to this subject matter? What kinds of interactions can occur between characters? Are they strategic or relational? What is the nature of these interactions—trust-based or resource-based? All of these aspects can be adjusted.

You can also adjust the pace of the interactions—making them more frequent at the beginning and less frequent toward the end—as well as set the proportions and values for different interaction types. Then, generate an outline, move on to the interaction script, and finally to video generation. If you feel something isn’t quite right along the way—for example, if a particular section isn’t exciting enough—you can change the direction, and it will rewrite the script accordingly.

Q: You mentioned "pleasure points." Can AI understand this concept, which serves human emotions and consciousness?

Kunpeng: AI is understandable because you feed it a large volume of scripts, and our professional team annotates them. This brings us to the issue of AI data: what kind of data anchors should you provide? Take blind testing, for example—humans need to give it feedback, otherwise it won’t know what “good” means.We generate two versions of the same content and have testers rate them: which one is better, whether it’s usable, and what the quality is like—but the testers don’t know which model wrote it.After repeated training and feedback, it becomes increasingly clear on these judgments. It knows what each model is capable of, and even which one excels at each step—which is better at branch design, and which is faster at advancing the plot.

Q: Are there already creators using this platform? Have you seen any particularly impressive ways it’s being used?

Kunpeng: During the testing phase, we released several hundred beta invitation codes to let creators try it out first; we haven’t started commercializing it to the public yet.I’ve seen some pretty interesting ways people are using it. For example, someone wrote their life story as a short biography and put it into the editor to generate branching choices—it’s kind of like using it to “tell fortunes.” I think that’s pretty funny.

Q: So it's not just a platform for making video games.

Kunpeng: Right. My ultimate conclusion is that it should be a “world.” Everyone is talking about open worlds, “Westworld,” and world models these days… but my view is that “Westworld” isn’t just about mountains, rivers, and the like—it has another very important aspect: the characters, relationships, events, and stories within it are constantly in motion.When interactive storytelling reaches its pinnacle, life itself becomes interactive storytelling—what I’m saying to you right now, whether I choose to say A or B next—choices are constantly present in life.Choice is the smallest unit through which humans engage with the world, and making a choice is essentially a form of annotation: what you like, what you don’t like, and what your preferences are at this very moment. When the choices generated by an infinite number of people, characters, and stories are all converted into data annotations, they can potentially become the model and agent that best understands “how a story should be written.” After all, stories are a timeless form of human emotional expression.

Broadly speaking, interactive movies and games are just one application of interactive storytelling, as are interactive short dramas.In the future, it could integrate more deeply with the gaming industry, with world models, and even with the kind of futuristic technology seen in *Ready Player One*—or with brain-computer interfaces. Ultimately, you still need a way to let users participate, make choices, and determine the course of the story. And the story paths users want to see are, in and of themselves, the highest-quality data.

03

The tipping point has been reached

Q: I’m curious about something. These days, people tend to instinctively view traditional short dramas and animated series as distinct from so-called “AI short dramas” and “AI animated series.” Will a similar situation arise with interactive video?

Kunpeng: I don’t think the distinction is that clear-cut. It’s just like the gaming industry: art is essentially just a medium used to convey what the creator truly wants to express.I think of AI as a virtual film set—it’s a virtual space for filming and production; on-location, real-world filming takes place on a tangible, physical set. Everyone does their own filming and expresses their own content.

It’s just that AI-generated content isn’t quite good enough yet—it still feels very “AI-like,” which is why we refer to it specifically as “AI content.” But as time goes on, I feel that this distinction has become very blurred. We’ve been conducting internal tests, and some of the recent results are so convincing that it’s hard to tell them apart from those created by real people.

Q: What exactly is being tested in this internal test?

Kunpeng: What we're measuring is when that so-called tipping point will arrive—the point at which we can use AI to generate content.

Q: As mentioned earlier, when you began focusing heavily on AI in 2023, were your employees eager to embrace it from the very beginning?

Kunpeng: It’s actually a process that’s both top-down and bottom-up—the two approaches converged. But at first, people were resistant because AI wasn’t good enough back then—which is perfectly understandable; it really wasn’t good enough at the beginning. It wasn’t until we kept trying that we realized it had actually become good enough.After June of last year, things changed dramatically: People began to realize that this technology had moved beyond the realm of concepts, demos, cost reduction, or preliminary materials and conceptual designs—it had truly become an “AI employee” capable of helping you get work done. By that point, people started using it on their own initiative.

Q: That makes sense—after all, people who create content tend to have high standards for it.

Kunpeng: Yes. So, taking our AltFlow as an example, I don’t see it as a replacement for creators. AI is there to empower creators, allowing them to focus on delivering a great user experience. As for some of the foundational tasks—such as writing flowcharts or designing branching paths—AI can handle them for you or provide excellent suggestions.I think with our current AI capabilities, AI can solve 70% to 80% of the problems, while the remaining 20% to 30% comes down to the creator’s inspiration—and that’s what’s most important about the creator themselves.

Q: In what directions will interactive content evolve in the coming years?

Kunpeng: I think there are three fairly clear directions.

First, greater social interaction. The evolution of games has followed a path from single-player to multiplayer, from offline to online, and finally to MMORPGs—becoming increasingly social. The same will be true for interactive content. By developing a two-player product, we aim to explore how social interaction will transform interactive storytelling.

Second, deeper integration with AI. AI will help creators better balance rational design and intuitive creativity, reduce costs, and empower everyone to explore topics they previously couldn’t afford to tackle.

Third, the formats will become more diverse. Interactive content shouldn’t be limited to live-action interactive games on Steam that last four or five hundred minutes. Shorter content, real-time live-streamed interactions, and procedurally generated content could all become new formats.

Q: What do you think the future of interactive storytelling will look like?

Kunpeng: I think a lot of science fiction works have actually already shown us this ultimate outcome—“Inception” is about creating dreams, allowing you to enter a world; “The Matrix” is about truly entering another reality through an interface; and in “Westworld,” every character has their own story, the entire world keeps running, and you’re the protagonist in it all.

I think interactive content in the future will be more like your very own “Westworld.” The IPs you love and the events that interest you can all be brought to life through AI and interaction, and you’ll be the protagonist in that world. You’ll no longer just passively consume stories—you’ll be able to truly participate in them.

I think that day is already very close. At the very least, if we set aside the more complex gameplay aspects and focus solely on the story, characters, and content generation, it’s already much closer than it used to be.

title: In 2026, the key to growth in the global gaming market lies in "monetization efficiency"
text:
It’s that time of year again—ChinaJoy. Major gaming industry forums and closed-door seminars are taking place one after another in Shanghai. After making the rounds at these events, I found that expanding into overseas markets remains a hot topic in the industry, but the focus of the discussions has fundamentally shifted.
This is closely tied to changes in the global gaming market. SensorTower’s previously released “State of Gaming 2026” report shows that total global mobile game downloads in 2025 declined by 7% year-over-year;Data from Adjust also indicates that in 2025, the cost per install (CPI) for global games rose by 30%, while the cost per click (CPC) increased by 33%.
These figures clearly demonstrate that the global gaming market has fully entered a phase of competition for existing users.With the traffic boom having peaked and customer acquisition costs continuing to rise, the model of relying solely on paid user acquisition is proving ineffective. Instead, the key to success in this new phase lies in whether developers can bypass the competitive red ocean of traditional channels to open up more diverse traffic sources, and whether they can fully leverage the value of traffic to truly boost monetization efficiency.
That’s precisely why, this year, the focus of our discussions has shifted from “how to invest” to “how to tap into opportunities”—tapping into more traffic sources externally and maximizing the monetization potential of every source of traffic internally.
At the Xsolla Connect Global Game Traffic and Marketing Growth Summit held on July 29, Xsolla presented a practical set of strategies to help global game developers address the new growth challenge of “expanding diverse traffic sources and improving monetization efficiency.”
01
Leveraging Influencers to Open New Growth Channels
In an era of competition for existing user bases, influencer marketing is becoming a key strategy for game developers expanding into overseas markets to broaden their traffic reach and build a diversified customer acquisition matrix. Numerous case studies in the gaming industry show that high-quality, co-created content produced by influencers—which engages their followers—often resonates more deeply with users than traditional hard advertising, effectively driving user growth and monetization.
However, the highly fragmented global influencer ecosystem has significantly raised the barrier to entry for influencer marketing. According to Teahouse’s findings, most brands generally encounter the following four major challenges during the actual implementation process: difficulty in accurately identifying suitable creators, difficulty in attributing results across platforms, a lack of unified coordination for large-scale campaigns, and complex compliance and settlement processes.Faced with these multiple obstacles, most brands can only treat influencer marketing as a supplementary source of user acquisition, conducting small-scale pilot campaigns; it is difficult for it to evolve into a stable and reliable channel for driving growth.
As a global leader in the video game e-commerce industry, Xsolla has not only recognized this industry challenge but has also integrated four core capabilities—influencer screening, performance attribution, campaign coordination, and cross-border settlement—into a unified workflow. As a result, the company has launched Xsolla Partner Network, a one-stop platform specifically designed to facilitate influencer and affiliate marketing partnerships.
Xsolla Partner Network
During the creator screening phase, Xsolla’s dedicated influencer marketing team can identify and establish business partnerships with a large number of niche influencers based on game genre, target market, and core audience profiles, completely freeing publishers from inefficient independent research and back-and-forth negotiations.
Once the promotion launches, this solution not only generates specialized tracking reports by game category and monitors key metrics—such as broadcast frequency, viewership, and peak concurrent viewers—on platforms like Twitch and YouTube in real time, but also includes the Creator Storefront, an exclusive online store for creators. It provides each partner influencer with a dedicated promotional page and a unique tracking link,allowing fans to place orders without having to navigate to an external site, while data on live stream exposure, watch time, and paid orders is fed back in real time. This makes it immediately clear which creators drive the most traffic and which have the highest conversion rates.
During large-scale promotional campaigns that require the simultaneous management of multiple influencers, brands can also create customized promotional tasks on the platform. By defining campaign durations and revenue-sharing ratios, they can distribute promotional materials, tracking links, and game redemption codes in bulk, while centrally managing the progress and performance metrics of all influencers—significantly reducing the administrative burden associated with coordinating a large number of influencers simultaneously.
More importantly, when it comes to fee settlement, Xsolla’s influencer marketing program uses a CPS (Cost Per Sale) revenue-sharing model . Brands can launch campaigns without any upfront costs and pay commissions only after influencers generate actual revenue. This minimizes the cost of trial and error while allowing brands to build their influencer marketing network with greater flexibility.At the same time, the most time-consuming aspects of cross-border transactions— global multi-currency commission calculations, cross-border payments, and regional compliance procedures—will all be handled centrally by the platform. With settlement barriers removed, influencers can truly lay the groundwork for sustainable, long-term success through their traffic generation.
Teahouse has learned that, through its intuitive and comprehensive backend interface and end-to-end support capabilities, Xsolla’s influencer marketing platform has helped numerous game developers efficiently set up and scale influencer marketing campaigns, effectively driving new user acquisition and overall revenue growth.For example, during the Early Access launch of the open-world MMO *Pax Dei*, the game team, with the support of Xsolla’s Influencer Marketing, rolled out a comprehensive influencer campaign, conducting a total of 1,291 livestreams with a combined watch time of nearly 600,000 hours.with peak concurrent viewers in live streams exceeding 24,000. In just 15 days, the campaign generated 18,200 game purchases, rapidly raising the game’s profile while building a substantial base of core early adopters.
02
Refined Advertising Monetization: Unlocking the Full Value of Existing Users
Expanding external traffic is only the first step toward growth. Once players start playing the game, figuring out how to fully unlock their commercial potential is also a key challenge for every company expanding overseas looking to break through revenue bottlenecks.
Industry data shows that among all gamers, over 90 percent of active users never make in-app purchases. In an industry environment where user acquisition costs continue to rise globally, the inability to monetize such a massive user base undoubtedly represents a massive waste of resources; however, forcing too many ad-based monetization points into a game will undermine the gaming experience and hinder revenue growth from core players as well as long-term retention.
On one hand, there is a monetization gap stemming from the massive number of non-paying users; on the other, traditional advertising models create a conflict between player retention and revenue. The industry has long lacked a solution that can balance revenue growth with player experience.In response, Xsolla Ads’ monetization and promotion solution offers a unique approach. By combining “unified identity recognition, voluntary value exchange, and advertising with rewards,” it builds a two-sided growth engine that connects player engagement with developer revenue.
The foundation of the entire system is Xsolla’s proprietary unified identity system: Xsolla ID. This is a unified identity profile that spans multiple devices and games, built by Xsolla over the past 20 years using data from 2.1 billion global players and over $4 billion in authentic payment records—all with the players’ authorization.
Therefore, unlike traditional advertising platforms that rely on algorithmic inferences to generate vague user tags, Xsolla can perform precise audience targeting based on actual in-app purchases and engagement behavior. Within the context of privacy compliance, it maintains stable and reliable data signals, enabling the precise differentiation of free-to-play users,casual players, and high-spending core users, and fully track the entire user journey—from ad engagement and item redemption to in-app purchase conversions—ensuring that every ad campaign is backed by clear, data-driven insights.
Building on this , Xsolla Ads has developed an ad display model driven by player choice: the Offerwall . The Offerwall can be implemented in various scenarios, such as mobile game web shops and in-game apps, allowing for precise targeting of high-quality users who are actively seeking in-game items and rewards in the scenarios where they are most active.
Unlike traditional ads—such as mandatory pop-ups or in-game interruptions—players actively choose whether to participate in all reward wall tasks. By completing tasks such as watching videos, trying out apps, or subscribing to services, users can redeem real rewards—such as in-game currency and limited-edition items—on their own terms. The entire process involves no forced exposure to ads and does not interrupt the main gameplay, thereby eliminating the negative impact of ads on the gaming experience at its source.
In addition to the full reward wall, Xsolla Ads also offers a "single offer" mode as a supplement. This mode precisely recommends a single high-value task to players at the most opportune moment, allowing players to see the offer at a glance and make decisions more directly. As a result, its conversion rate can even surpass that of the full reward wall.
This “participation-for-rewards” value exchange mechanism can easily drive new user acquisition, reactivate existing users, and monetize the user base.Data shows that 93% of paying players who use reward walls continue to make purchases in the mobile game’s in-app store, which clearly demonstrates that reward walls not only do not divert high-spending players but actually effectively drive incremental value from core players.Furthermore, players who participate in reward walls see their D7–D30 retention rates increase by approximately 40%, and the probability of subsequent in-app purchases rises by 10 to 14 times. This can be said to truly achieve a positive feedback loop among monetization, retention, and spending.
The integration process for the rewards wall is very simple and convenient. It requires no complex coding or high R&D costs and can be easily launched and activated in just a matter of minutes.At the same time, the platform supports various performance-based billing models, including CPI, CPE, MRCPE, and CPC. Combined with industry-leading ad revenue-sharing policies, it can effectively monetize active free-to-play users who previously generated no revenue, opening up a stable source of incremental revenue for games.
Over the past few years, Xsolla Ads has delivered significant revenue growth for its partners: total revenue increased by 5%, payment transaction volume rose by 37%, the number of Web Shop (mobile game in-app purchase store) users grew by 35%, and the number of paying users increased by 30%. Notably, after Tilting Point integrated a reward wall into the *Star Trek: Timelines* in-game store, the number of in-game store users grew by 30%, and the total number of paying users increased by 8.5%; payment transaction volume rose by 10%, and the in-game store’s total revenue also increased by 5%.

A Gathering of Industry Leaders: A Comprehensive Look at New Opportunities for Global Expansion
In addition, the summit brought together senior professionals from leading companies across the entire global gaming industry chain—including RTB House, Tencent Cloud, OEG, Tenjin, and Xiaomi—who shared insights on real-world practical scenarios such as high-quality traffic and advertising, exploring emerging markets (Vietnam), omnichannel monetization, and global distribution.
Jakub Gajewski, Head of New Business for Games at RTB House, delivered a presentation titled “The Core Value of High-Quality Traffic and Data Privacy in the Current Advertising Ecosystem.” He noted that while many advertising teams focus solely on click-through rates and user quality, they often overlook underlying issues such as failed redirects, which continuously erode the overall return on ad spend.To address this challenge, he introduced a proven and practical implementation plan that leverages first-party data to build a retargeting advertising system. While strictly adhering to data privacy compliance standards, this approach helps brands achieve efficient and stable overseas advertising campaigns.

Kelly Wu, Senior Business Manager of Tencent Cloud’s Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and International Business Division, delivered a presentation titled “Tencent Cloud International: Full-Stack AI Practical Insights—Boosting Efficiency with AI Tools to Reshape the Full Gaming Value Chain in the Asia-Pacific Region.”She explained that Tencent Cloud has built an end-to-end AI solution for the gaming industry based on the TOKEN HUB large-model aggregation platform and centered around the Hun Yuan large model. Leveraging tools such as CodeBuddy, Media AI,Voice AI Agent, ACE Anti-Cheat, and WeTest, the solution empowers the entire gaming lifecycle—from R&D and marketing to player services, security protection, and product testing—helping companies expanding overseas leverage AI to reduce costs, improve efficiency, and build a competitive edge in the Asia-Pacific market.
In addition, Henry Li Mingzhe, Global Head of Growth at Tenjin, focused on new trends in cross-border growth for 2026. He analyzed changes in revenue structures driven by category rotation and hybrid monetization, shared insights on the shift in campaign measurement from CPI to ROAS, and discussed the application of predicted LTV (pLTV) in budget decision-making.Tenjin is a leading global mobile attribution and growth analytics platform, currently serving over 60,000 active games and apps worldwide and monitoring nearly $200 million in monthly ad spend;Chen Guanhong, International Business Manager at Xiaomi’s Business Cooperation Department, provided a detailed analysis of the Xiaomi App Store’s ecosystem advantages. By fully leveraging the strengths of the manufacturer and the enabling capabilities of the operating system, and drawing on Xiaomi’s extensive overseas user base, the company is deeply committed to diversifying business models—including user acquisition and IAP (in-app purchases)—to provide comprehensive business solutions for developer partners and create abundant growth opportunities.
A group of industry partners shared practical, first-hand insights on key aspects of global expansion, explored growth opportunities from various perspectives, and clearly outlined the future direction of the global gaming market amid a competitive landscape dominated by existing players. It is safe to say that this summit combined high-level industry perspectives with actionable guidance and was packed with valuable insights.
Conclusion
As the host of this summit, Xsolla has introduced a growth solution for global expansion that directly addresses core pain points and covers the entire game operations lifecycle.In addition to XPN influencer marketing and Xsolla Ads monetization—which were highlighted earlier—IP licensing services are also a crucial component of this growth ecosystem. The former focuses on monetizing existing users, while the latter addresses the need to “build brand equity” beyond traffic and monetization.
According to reports, Xsolla’s IP licensing service enables domestic game developers to gain direct access to top-tier global entertainment IPs—including Hollywood films and TV shows as well as renowned sports franchises—thereby completely overcoming the challenges associated with traditional IP partnerships, such as limited distribution channels, lengthy review cycles, and cumbersome partnership terms.As a result, developers can leverage high-quality IP partnerships to effectively reduce overseas customer acquisition costs, stimulate player spending, and simultaneously build and consolidate long-term brand equity.
Xsolla’s three core business areas—influencer marketing, advertising, and IP licensing—work in tandem to provide global brands with a standardized, end-to-end growth solution that is actionable and reusable.
By leveraging Xsolla’s influencer marketing to expand the boundaries of diversified traffic growth, utilizing Xsolla Ads for precision operations to revitalize existing users and enhance monetization efficiency, and breaking down collaboration barriers with global top-tier content assets through IP licensing services, Xsolla has fully established a closed-loop growth model for global expansion: “New User Acquisition — revenue growth from existing users — long-term asset accumulation.” This solution systematically addresses the pain points of expensive user acquisition and unstable growth, truly transforming global game expansion from “high-cost trial and error” to “certain growth,” making global operations more hassle-free and stable.
It is worth noting that during this year’s ChinaJoy, teams from Xsolla’s three major business lines have gathered in Shanghai . Developers interested in building a sustainable overseas growth system and enhancing their comprehensive global expansion capabilities can take this opportunity to engage in in-depth face-to-face discussions and explore partnerships, working together to uncover new opportunities for game globalization in a highly competitive market.

title: A Conversation with League of Legends: Using "Classics" to Bring Back Players' Youth
text:
Nostalgia has been a constant theme in the gaming industry in recent years.
People generally tend to be nostalgic, and with the help of memory—the best filter of all—the time spent playing games, filled with happy and carefree emotions, becomes even more precious.
So, when remakes of classic games and nostalgia servers for online games are released, bringing back memories of players’ youth, developers can also reap positive word-of-mouth and commercial returns.
Seen this way, nostalgia is, to some extent, a win-win situation for both developers and players.
Of course, this assumes that the developer isn’t simply capitalizing on nostalgia for marketing purposes. True nostalgia should allow players to genuinely reconnect with that joy and add a new sense of delight to it.
On July 12, during the 2026 League of Legends Mid-Season Invitational, Riot Games chose to unveil Classic Mode—essentially a “retro server”—through an exhibition match, signaling its imminent return to the Rift.
To be honest, when I saw the Rift with its retro textures, a Scorpion that could one-shot an opponent with just 33 Qs, and the abstract concept art for Amumu—it should have been a scene that brought tears to the eyes of old-school players,but for some reason, I found myself thinking of those old, patina-covered internet cafes—which are now a rare sight—and a group of people whose faces have long since faded from my memory.
It's a very strange feeling, as if you've seen your past self and suddenly realized that it was already ten years ago.
But in the exhibition match, this Rift—which I once knew so well—seemed slightly different from how I remembered it; for example, the Snowman and the Cookie had been visually redesigned.
This suggests that Riot isn't simply rolling back *League of Legends* to a previous version; the "Classic Mode," which has been officially announced to launch on July 30, includes quite a few new design elements.
Actually, one day in June, at the invitation of League of Legends, I attended an in-person media demo of Classic Mode and had a chat with the project team.
In the trial match, I used the "Steam Robot" to transform into the "Rice Cooker Robot." Although I didn't manage to lure many opponents, I still managed to control the Thunder and Lightning map thanks to the return of the "Banner of Command" item.
Veteran players should be very familiar with this item—its purpose is to upgrade a sports car into a “Plus” version. Although the Dragon buff didn’t originally provide lane-pushing capabilities, the Classic server has retained this design. When the two effects stack, you’ll find that the sports car becomes a powerful push tool.
Beyond-Line-of-Sight Tower Destruction
To be honest, it’s precisely the chemistry created by the clash between these old items and modern mechanics that makes Classic Mode feel like more than just a trip down memory lane. This iteration of League of Legends’ Classic Mode exudes a sense of freshness—a blend of the old and the new—at every turn.
Today, League of Legends' Classic Mode officially launched. Based on my previous hands-on experience, I’ve gained some insight into Riot’s “two-pronged” approach—that is, recreating the feel of the “past” while firmly embracing the “modern” experience.
01
Bringing the “Past” Back to Life
To recreate the feelings of the past, you must, of course, start with visual memories.
Since its launch, *League of Legends* has undergone numerous iterations—not only in the visual design of its hundreds of champions, but also in the client itself. Therefore, recreating the original visuals is the first step in *League of Legends*’ Classic Mode’s journey to revisit the “past.”
With its familiar interface, classic hero portraits, and the long-missed equipment bar, Classic Mode has essentially recreated the original experience faithfully.
Plus, when I reopened the interface, I saw the old system from 17 years ago—where you had to manually set up your rune page and the old-style talent page before entering the queue, including red, yellow, and blue runes, Essences, War Zeal, Storm Rider’s Surge,Decree of the Thunderlord, plus a 21/0/9 build—to be honest, all I can say is, “It’s back—it’s all back!”
The map designers did their archaeological homework thoroughly, recreating the early-game terrain and neutral monsters of the Rift—including Baron Nashor, who looks more like a slug than a dragon; small dragons that grant gold to the entire team instead of a dragon buff; and the trio of red and blue buffs.
Classic Mode recreates a version of the game that roughly corresponds to the timeline between Season 3 and Season 4. The development team told me: “‘The version that received the most votes from players and is considered the most representative of that glorious era is the Season 3 World Championship version; what players can actually experience in Classic Mode is primarily the Season 3 World Championship version, followed by versions up to Season 1 of Season 4.’”
Why this range?
The project team explained that internally at Riot, Seasons 1 through 4 are collectively defined as “an era” because the Hextech Engine underwent a major update around that time, and it was only after that update that the map and graphics entered a more modern phase. Therefore, the selection of this time period is based both on the company’s internal definition of the “classic era” and on global player surveys.
I, too, got into the game right around the time of the S3 World Championship. In a sense, that year marked the beginning of *League of Legends* igniting the global esports scene; names like Faker, UZI, and Wuwukai—which would later become household names—first came to the world’s attention at that time.
As for the champions, there are actually many more that won’t be launching alongside Classic Mode. The development team has admitted that champions with particularly difficult-to-rework skill sets will have to be brought back gradually at a later date. With that in mind, highly anticipated classic *League of Legends* champions like the original Gunner, Swordmaiden, and Blade Mistress should also make their return to the Rift someday.
I also learned that this time, Classic Mode is being led by Riot’s global studio in Sydney, and this team “wasn’t created entirely from scratch.” To do justice to this mode, which holds such sentimental value for players, they brought back many veteran designers who had left during Seasons 2 and 3 to contribute to the project,one of whom happened to be the designer responsible for that specific version back then and has now returned to lead Hextech and overall design.
The original version of Classic Mode was actually a demo that Riot put together on their own during an internal "hackathon." They said the veteran employees had a blast playing it, which is why it gradually evolved into the full-fledged mode we see today.
As for the “modern” elements interspersed within the recreation of the “past,”for example, regarding the Dragon buff I mentioned earlier—which strengthens the lane—the project team stated that they had tested several versions and found that while some players did want a more “authentic” retro experience, the majority of players felt that if it were too authentic, the time commitment would be too high for modern players.
It’s true that back then, the pace of *League of Legends* was slower; minion and jungle camp respawn times were longer than they are now, and there were no map resources like the Herald to speed up the game. A single match could take 40 to 50 minutes, or even over an hour, and Riot felt that this didn’t align with modern players’ gaming habits.
And this brings us right to what I was saying about the “modernity” of League of Legends’ Classic mode.
02
Connecting with "Now"
If nostalgia sets the emotional tone for a product or gameplay experience, then a key question for developers is how to ensure it doesn’t become “outdated.” After all, this is what truly determines whether a product or gameplay experience is more than just “cashing in on nostalgia.”
What sets "League of Legends" Classic Mode apart from "museum-style" retro content is primarily its commitment to modernity.
Nostalgia doesn't have to mean suffering—Riot Games understands this very well.
For example, the previous rune system—while I felt it had some elements of meta-game strategy—lacked depth, and design choices such as requiring in-game currency to purchase runes and unlocking slots as you leveled up were truly outdated for that era.
At the time, this was extremely grueling for new players, so Classic Mode incorporated a clever system to lighten the load. First, the system automatically provides two rune pages carefully curated by designers,saving players the time and effort of grinding. Furthermore, this system is tied to a pass similar to the Hextech Brawl Pass, where core content—such as rune pages and editing permissions—can be earned through gameplay. By playing Classic Mode, players can generally obtain more than 10 rune pages for free.
The current version’s matchmaking, in-map markers, skill pre-input, and even optional WASD movement have all been added to Classic Mode.
Furthermore, in light of the significant differences between S3 and the current version in terms of the jungle and support roles, the project team has confirmed that the Chinese server will provide tutorial content. They’ve even included a little Easter egg: they may invite familiar commentators and video creators from back in the day to return and reintroduce the Classic server to players. “Otherwise, players will be completely lost when they arrive, and losing them would have a huge impact on us.”.
The Three Departments have already held a joint trial.
In terms of product design, Classic Mode wasn’t developed as a standalone client; instead, it was directly integrated into the existing League of Legends client. Just as you can access Teamfight Tactics by opening the client, there will be an entry point for Classic Mode in the existing client once it launches.
When asked about the toughest challenge in the entire project, the project team’s answer was straightforward: hero balance.
The logic is easy to understand: if the team is only maintaining the current version, all they have to worry about are a few overpowered heroes.
However, Classic Mode launched with 60 heroes all at once—each from different historical versions—so the entire meta had to be built almost from scratch, while also leaving room for heroes to be added later.
The project team admitted that the version we played in Shanghai that day wasn’t actually balanced; some heroes were even temporarily locked and unavailable for selection because they hadn’t been fine-tuned yet,and the game’s pace was constantly being adjusted. They also confirmed that the numerical structure of Classic Mode largely follows the original settings from Season 3, though many champions’ abilities have changed so much over the years that they need to be gradually restored to their original forms.
However, when it comes to balance, Riot has set a very clear tone: entertainment comes first, with less emphasis on competitiveness.
When it comes to those powerful champions that used to provide such an exhilarating gameplay experience—such as AP Yasuo, Q-Silence Kassadin, and Control-Dragon Iron Man—teams prefer to preserve their unique characteristics and the thrill they offer, rather than nerfing them to a bland, run-of-the-mill state based on modern standards.
After all, when it comes to Nostalgia Mode, the moments that really make veteran players smile are still scenes like the old Sejuani spamming QW to stack up AP, then using her W to instantly take down the ADC.
So, in reality, Classic Mode strikes a balance between “pure nostalgia” and “playability,” leaning more toward the latter. Riot has preserved the map and the era’s atmosphere, but has also smoothed out the most frustrating aspects.
At this point, some of you might be wondering: since there are plans for future updates, how do you decide which heroes will return first and which ones later?
Actually, the answer is a player vote.
The project team revealed that a voting portal will be opened shortly after Classic Mode goes live, and players will be able to request specific heroes, items, and even classic gameplay from a particular era.
Classic maps like Crystal Scar and Twisted Treeline, as well as designs like Garen as the main antagonist—which evoke strong nostalgic memories—will be considered for inclusion as long as there is enough demand. They also mentioned that, due to the massive player base in China, votes from Chinese players carry significant weight; content that Chinese players particularly want will be prioritized internally by Riot.
As for monetization—the issue that has drawn the most public attention—the project team has taken a surprisingly restrained approach. They say there won’t be any special designs; it will mainly consist of a collection of classic skins.
Many of these skins feature old designs that have not been seen since the heroes were reworked or their concept art was updated. They will be remade to match the original versions, preserving the classic concept art while making only minor updates to the visual effects. The team has completely remade them to faithfully recreate their original appearance, complete with the classic chromas exclusive to these classic skins.
The genius of League of Legends’ Classic Mode lies in the fact that it was never intended to be a sealed-off museum from the start. Riot has integrated it into the main client’s product structure, curated its content carefully, and established an update schedule driven by player votes. Taken together, these elements point to a single philosophy:to make nostalgia something that grows gradually and coexists with the present over the long term.
Conclusion
While writing this article, I often found myself wondering: What does the nostalgia surrounding *League of Legends* mean to players?
Later, I realized that after becoming deeply embedded in the esports scene, *League of Legends*’ updates have tended to lean toward the esports side. The main reason why previous champions were so talked about by players was that they “dominated a specific lane.”such as the “undefeatable AP Master Yi” or “unbeatable Irelia with Blade Waltz”—all of which, from a competitive standpoint, are highly unbalanced, overpowered champions.
However, for the majority of players, beyond the competitive aspect of *League of Legends*, the game is really more about finding enjoyment. As for the emotional resonance of Classic Mode, rather than attributing it to players’ nostalgia for a specific item, it’s more accurate to say they’re nostalgic for a time when everything was still simple.
Back then, when we played the game, there was no thought given to controlling the dragon, no attention to laning details or strategic gameplay—nobody really knew how to play. Most people would just pick a champion, head to a lane, last-hit minions, and fight.
Perhaps my fondness for the Classic mode stems from the fact that Riot has brought back memories of my carefree youth.

title: The sequel to *Late Ming* will continue to be developed by Xia Siyuan's team, with support from 505Games
text:
505 Games announced today (the 29th) that it has entered into a partnership with Chengdu Recursive Dolphin Technology Co., Ltd. for the development and publication of the sequel to the *Wuchang* series.Recursive Dolphin was founded by Xia Siyuan, the lead creator of *Late Ming: Feathers of the Abyss*. This means that even after the IP changed hands and the core team left their original company, creative control over the *Wuchang* series remains with its original creator.
It has been exactly one year since the release of *Late Ming: Feathers of the Void*. On its first day of release, the game surpassed 131,000 concurrent players on Steam, and the cumulative player count across PC and console platforms has now reached 5 million. It should be noted that this figure includes players who gained access through Xbox Game Pass and PlayStation Plus subscription services and does not represent pure sales figures.
In April of this year, Digital Bros, the parent company of 505 Games, completed the acquisition of the intellectual property rights for *Impermanence*, a deal that sparked considerable discussion within the industry at the time. The outright acquisition of a Chinese game IP by an overseas publisher is still a relatively rare occurrence in the domestic gaming industry. Three months later, 505 Games immediately announced plans for a sequel—a remarkably swift move.
In terms of the partnership model, the sequel will be developed primarily by Chengdu Recursive Dolphin, with 505 Games providing financial support and handling global distribution. At the same time, Digital Bros will establish a wholly-owned subsidiary in Chengdu to work in close collaboration with Recursive Dolphin. This “local studio + local subsidiary” setup demonstrates 505’s long-term commitment to this IP.
For Xia Siyuan’s team, continuing to refine the IP they created from scratch as an independent studio—with overseas publishers covering distribution resources and funding—is actually a pretty good option compared to the traditional choices of “selling out to a major studio” or “continuing to struggle through independent development and self-publishing.” Although they no longer own the IP, they retain creative control and are no longer burdened by financial pressure.
The decision to have the same team develop the sequel to *Impermanence* rather than start from scratch also indirectly demonstrates that 505 Games recognizes the foundation laid by the first game and the irreplaceable value of Xia Siyuan’s team.
In the late Ming Dynasty, its foreign name was Wuchang.
However, sequels are always put to the test by the “second-installment curse.”The proportion of the first game’s 5 million players who subscribed, along with the payment conversion rate, will determine the true commercial potential of this IP. The shift from the “sense of surprise” in the first game to “managing expectations” for the sequel presents a significant challenge for a new studio that has just become independent.
The story of *Impermanence* is far from over; the storyteller is still here.

title: 鸡否？上号！2026和平精英吃鸡节重磅开启！重庆上演全城狂欢
text:
当一句“鸡否？”成为特种兵之间的集结暗号，一场贯穿线上和线下，横跨“海岛”与重庆的盛大狂欢正式拉开大幕！
2026和平精英吃鸡节重磅登场，由7733万票选出的人气地图龙狮城随「激战金秋」版本焕新回归；海量福利、明星达人、线下活动《吃鸡的一天》同步解锁。这一次，吃鸡文化走出屏幕，邀全体特种兵共赴一场欢聚盛宴。
